title: Virtual Triage B
subtitle: 4-year-old with a minor injury — triaging down safely
stem: Sunday evening, 6:15 pm. A father walks in holding a crying 4-year-old boy with a blood-stained towel on his head. You are the triage nurse. The waiting area already has eleven children.
parent: "He fell off the dining chair about 20 minutes ago and hit his head on the floor. There was a lot of blood. He cried straight away. He hasn't vomited. He's been talking to me the whole way here."

vitals.note: Crying loudly but stops when father speaks to him, pushes your hand away, walked in holding father's hand. 2 cm laceration over the left parietal scalp, oozing, no active bleeding. Pupils equal and reactive. No other injury.

decisions.title: Impression
decisions.prompt: From the doorway: a loud cry that settles when his father speaks, fighting you off, walked in; breathing normal; pink. What is your impression — stable or unstable, life-threatening or not?

options.text: Stable — PAT normal; minor head injury with a scalp wound
options.outcome: You settle on a reassuring first impression and move to a focused assessment.
options.note: A loud, consolable cry with normal tone and interaction is a reassuring appearance; a child who walked in and pushes you away is not critically unwell. Stable on the PAT means you have time for a focused assessment — it does not mean "nothing to do".

options.text: Unstable — neurological: raised intracranial pressure from the head injury
options.outcome: You rush him into the resuscitation bay. He stops crying when his father speaks to him and starts pulling at the monitor leads. The team asks why he is there.
options.note: Crying is not an abnormal appearance; it is the expected response of a frightened 4-year-old in pain. CNS dysfunction on the PAT means abnormal appearance with normal breathing and circulation: drowsy, floppy, not interacting, or a high-pitched inconsolable cry.

options.text: Unstable — circulation: shock from blood loss
options.outcome: You ask for IV access and fluid. He fights the cannulation; the waiting list grows while a well-perfused child takes up your time.
options.note: Scalp wounds bleed dramatically, but his circulation side is normal: pink, warm, CRT 1 s, HR 112. A towel of blood looks like more than it is. Shock from a scalp laceration alone is very rare in a 4-year-old.

options.text: Unstable — breathing affected: he is breathing fast
options.outcome: You put an oxygen mask on him. He pulls it off and cries harder. Once settled on his father's lap his breathing is quiet and regular at 24.
options.note: Crying raises the rate but there is no flaring, no recession, no abnormal sound. Work of breathing is normal. Count the rate again once he settles.

decisions.key: Stable — PAT normal; no immediate threat. Minor head injury with a scalp laceration.

decisions.title: Intervention
decisions.prompt: He is stable on the PAT, so you have time. What is your intervention now?

options.text: Clean and dress the wound first, then ask about the fall
options.outcome: Ten minutes go into cleaning and dressing the wound. The head-injury screen still has not been done, and the next child is waiting.
options.note: Wound care can wait a few minutes; the head-injury screen cannot. If he needs a CT or a doctor urgently, you must know now.

options.text: Head-injury screen: mechanism and height of fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting (how many times), drowsiness or unusual behaviour, seizure, headache; examine the scalp for a boggy swelling and check pupils; then a full set of vital signs
options.outcome: Fall from about 60 cm, cried at once, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, behaving normally. No boggy swelling; pupils equal and reactive. HR 108, RR 24, SpO₂ 98 %, BP 98/62.
options.note: A fall of under 1 metre with immediate cry, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting, normal behaviour, equal pupils and no boggy haematoma puts him in the low-risk group. Vital signs complete the picture.

options.text: Send him straight for a CT head; every head injury with bleeding needs imaging
options.outcome: Radiology asks for the doctor's request and the indication. You have neither; he waits in the corridor for 30 minutes.
options.note: A CT is a doctor's decision, and a low-mechanism fall with no red flags does not need one. Unnecessary CT exposes a 4-year-old to radiation. Your job is to screen and report.

options.text: Give an anti-emetic and paracetamol now so he is comfortable in the queue
options.outcome: Anti-emetic and paracetamol given. He is comfortable — and if he vomits later, the drug may hide it.
options.note: Paracetamol is reasonable, but an anti-emetic would mask vomiting, which is one of your re-triage signs. Do not treat the symptom you are relying on to detect deterioration.

decisions.key: Focused head-injury assessment first — mechanism and height of fall, loss of consciousness, vomiting, behaviour, seizure, headache; scalp and pupils — with a full set of vital signs; wound care after that.
must: head-injury screen or neurological check before wound care

decisions.title: Triage category
decisions.prompt: No loss of consciousness, no vomiting, alert and playing with his father's phone, pupils equal, a small laceration that has stopped oozing, vitals normal. Which level?

options.text: Level 2 · Emergent — any head injury with a wound, to be safe
options.outcome: He takes the Level 2 cubicle. Ten minutes later a wheezing child arrives and has to wait in a chair.
options.note: Over-triage has a cost: he takes a Level 2 slot while a child with breathing difficulty waits. Triage is about matching urgency to need, in both directions. Reserve Level 2 for red flags.

options.text: Level 4 · Less urgent — wound closure by the doctor, observation in the waiting area, re-triage if anything changes
options.outcome: Level 4. He sits with his father, playing on the phone, within your sight.
options.note: A low-risk head injury with a laceration needing closure is Level 4: seen within the hour, father told the warning signs, and you re-check him on your waiting-area rounds. Triaging down confidently is as important as triaging up.

options.text: Level 5 · Non-urgent — put a dressing on and send him to the OPD tomorrow
options.outcome: His father is handed a dressing and told to come to OPD tomorrow. At the door he turns back: "Is nobody going to stitch it?"
options.note: The laceration needs closure today, and a head injury needs a doctor's assessment and documented advice before discharge. Level 5 sends him away without either.

options.text: Level 3 · Urgent — in case he deteriorates
options.outcome: Level 3. He will be seen a little sooner, but no one has yet told the father what to watch for.
options.note: Defensible if your waiting area is unmonitored, but with no red flags the evidence supports Level 4 with clear re-triage criteria. Whichever level, what matters is that the re-triage triggers are set and the father knows them.

decisions.title: Advice to the family while they wait
decisions.prompt: Father asks: "Is he going to be all right? What should I watch for?" What do you tell him?

options.text: "He's fine, don't worry, just wait for your turn."
options.outcome: The father nods and sits down. He does not know what to watch for.
options.note: Reassurance without instructions. The father is your best observer for the next hour; give him a job.

options.text: "He looks well now. Come straight to me if he vomits, becomes drowsy or hard to wake, behaves strangely, has a fit, complains of a worsening headache, or if the wound starts bleeding again. Keep him sitting with you; no running about. I'll check on him every 15 minutes."
options.outcome: The father repeats the warning signs back to you and sits where you can see them both.
options.note: Specific warning signs in plain words, what to do if they appear, and a promise of regular review. This is family-centred care and it is also your safety net.

options.text: "Keep him awake at all costs; if he sleeps he could slip into a coma."
options.outcome: The father shakes the boy awake every few minutes. The child is tired and crying, and the father is frightened.
options.note: A myth that frightens parents. A tired 4-year-old may sleep; what matters is that he is rousable. Teach the father to check that he wakes normally, not to keep him awake.

options.text: Hand him the printed head-injury leaflet and move to the next patient
options.outcome: The father glances at the leaflet and folds it into his pocket.
options.note: A leaflet supports a conversation; it does not replace one. Many parents will not read it, and he needs to know to come to you, not just to "seek help".

decisions.title: Re-triage
decisions.prompt: Forty minutes later the father comes to the desk: "Sister, he has vomited twice and now he wants to sleep." What do you do?

options.text: "Vomiting is common after a fright; let him sleep, the doctor will see him soon."

vitals.note: Drowsy, rouses to voice, pupils equal, HR falling.

options.outcome: Twenty minutes later the father shouts from the waiting area: the boy is very hard to wake. HR 68, rouses only to pain, left pupil slightly larger than the right.
options.note: Two vomits and new drowsiness after a head injury are red flags. This is exactly the change your advice was designed to catch. Act on it.

options.text: Bring him to a monitored bed, repeat the PAT and ABCDE with pupils, upgrade to Level 2 and call the doctor now with an ISBAR handover: "4-year-old, head injury 1 hour ago, now vomited twice and drowsy, I need you here now"

vitals.note: Drowsy but rousable, pupils equal, no further vomiting. Doctor at the bedside in 4 minutes.

options.outcome: On a monitored bed: drowsy but rousable, pupils equal, HR 96, no further vomiting. The doctor is at the bedside in 4 minutes and a CT is arranged.
options.note: Triage is dynamic: a change in the child changes the category. Re-assess, upgrade, escalate with numbers and a timeframe. The earlier advice to the father is what brought him to you in time.

options.text: Give an anti-emetic and put him back in the queue
options.outcome: After the anti-emetic he sleeps in the queue. On your next round he rouses only to voice and HR is 64.
options.note: Treating the symptom hides the sign. Vomiting after head injury is information, not a nuisance.

options.text: Move him up one level to Level 3 and let the doctor know at the next round
options.outcome: Level 3. The doctor is at the far end of the department and will see him on the round. Fifteen minutes later he is harder to wake.
options.note: Red flags after head injury go to Level 2 with the doctor called now, not informed later.

debrief: Why is triaging down correctly as important as triaging up? What happens to the department when every child is Level 2?
Which single piece of advice to the father made the difference at the 40-minute mark?
List the head-injury red flags you would teach a new triage nurse.
takeHome: A stable PAT buys time for a focused assessment; it does not end the assessment.
Screen head injuries for red flags before wound care.
Triage down with confidence when there are no red flags — and set re-triage triggers.
Give parents specific warning signs and a route back to you.
Triage is dynamic: a change in the child changes the level, and the doctor is called now.
references: AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: Pediatric Assessment Triangle.
NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management (2023): red flags in children.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 01: triage levels, DIRECT approach.

ending.smooth: The CT shows a small extradural haematoma. The neurosurgeon operates that night; because the change was caught early he goes home on day 4 with no deficit.
ending.detour: The CT shows an extradural haematoma. He reaches theatre, but later and drowsier than he should have, and his recovery is slower.
